questions.html:
Suppose we want to implement a stack data structure using just one queue. push() and pop() are two functions on stack that may use enqueue() and dequeue() functions of queue Q.

Which of the following pair(s) of implementations for push() and pop() work?

options.html:
def push(x, Q): 
        Q.enqueue(x) 


 def pop(Q): 
        for k in range(1, len(Q)):
                Q.enqueue(Q.dequeue())
                return Q.dequeue()

def push(x, Q): 
        Q.enqueue(x) 
        for k in range(1, len(Q)):
                Q.enqueue(Q.dequeue())


 def pop(Q): 
        return Q.dequeue()

def push(x, Q): 
        Q.enqueue(x) 
        for k in range(1, len(Q)):
                Q.enqueue(Q.dequeue())


def pop(Q): 
        for k in range(1, len(Q)):
                Q.enqueue(Q.dequeue())
                return Q.dequeue()

def push(x, Q): 
        Q.enqueue(x) 


def pop(Q): 
        return Q.dequeue()

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Queue is FIFO and Stack is LIFO.

To implement a stack using one queue – 

We can have 2 different approaches viz make pop() efficient and push() costly or pop() costly and push() efficient.

1. pop() efficient and push() costly – 

To pop() we can directly dequeue().

*** We’re directly dequeing to pop() from stack. So, we’ve to maintain most recently pushed element in the front and least recently pushed element in the rear of queue. To achieve this ie to push(x), we simply enqueue(x). This will make most recently added element in the rear. And to bring this element to the front, we’ve to do (n-1) enqueue( dequeue() ). ***

To push(x) we’ve to first enqueue(x) and then perform (n-1) times enqueue( dequeue() ). (considering, n is the size of queue after enqueue())

2. pop() costly and push() efficient – 

To push(x) we can directly enqueue(x).

*** Most recently pushed element is in the rear and least recently pushed element is in the front of the queue. If we directly do dequeue() then we’ll get least recently pushed element, but according to stack LIFO property we should be getting most recently pushed element. So, to achieve this, we do (n-1) enqueue( dequeue() ) this will bring most recently pushed element to the front of the queue. Now, one dequeue() will give required element. ***

To pop() we’ve to first perform (n-1) times enqueue( dequeue() ) and then dequeue(). (considering, n is the size of queue)

Option A : This is implementation of approach 2.

Option B : This is implementation of approach 1.

Option C : This is working as a Queue. (I’m not explaining this, but you can think about this, good exercise)

Option D : This is working as a Queue.

Answer :- A, B.

Consider the following pseudocode of function mystery() which takes one stack orig_stack as input and modify its content using another stack calles helper_stack

def mystery(orig_stack): 
      helper_stack = Stack()
      while orig_stack: # not empty
             element = orig_stack.pop() 
             while helper_stack and helper_stack.top() < element:
                         orig_stack.push(helper_stack.pop()) 
             helper_stack.push(element)
 
      while helper_stack: 
             orig_stack.push(helper_stack.pop())


Suppose the content of orig_stack initially is $-1, 7, 0, 3, -2,$ where $-1$ is on the top.

What will be the content of orig_stack() after the function call mystery()?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Answer is Option : A

In mystery(),

  • The first while loop, transfers all elements from orig_stack to helper_stack such that elements in helper_stack is in sorted order at the end of the loop. And top() of helper_stack is the least element.

  • The second while loop, pops all elements form helper_stack and pushes those in orig_stack, one by one. Thus, at the end of the loop, orig_stack will have elements in reverse sorted order. And top() of orig_stack is the greatest element.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

 

Initial Setup

Initial state:

orig_stack = [-1, 7, 0, 3, -2]  (top is `-1`)
helper_stack = []  (empty)

Step-by-Step Execution

Iteration 1: Processing -1

  • Pop -1 from orig_stack.
    • orig_stack = [7, 0, 3, -2]
    • element = -1
  • Compare -1 with helper_stack.top() (helper_stack is empty, so no comparison is needed).
  • Push -1 into helper_stack.
    • helper_stack = [-1]

Iteration 2: Processing 7

  • Pop 7 from orig_stack.
    • orig_stack = [0, 3, -2]
    • element = 7
  • Compare 7 with helper_stack.top() (-1):
    • Since 7 > -1
  • Push 7 into helper_stack.
    • helper_stack = [7]
    • orig_stack = [-1, 0, 3, -2]

Iteration 3: Processing -1

  • Pop -1 from orig_stack.
    • orig_stack = [0, 3, -2]
    • element = -1
  • Compare -1 with helper_stack.top() (7):
    • Since -1 < 7
    • orig_stack = [0, 3, -2]
    • helper_stack = [-1, 7]

Iteration 4: Processing 0

  • Pop 3 from orig_stack.
    • orig_stack = [3, -2]
    • element = 0
  • Compare 0 with helper_stack.top() (-1):
    • Since 0 > -1,
    • orig_stack = [-1, 3, -2]
    • helper_stack = [0, 7]

Iteration 5: Processing -1

  • Pop -2 from orig_stack.
    • orig_stack = [3, -2]
    • element = -1
  • Compare -1 with helper_stack.top() (0):
    • Since 0 > -1,
    • orig_stack = [3, -2]
    • helper_stack = [-1, 0, 7]

 

..... Option A is Correct ans.

  • getMax() is a function that returns the maximum without deleting it.
  • StackWithMax is implemented using a singly linked list, and each node of the linked list has $3$ fields to store.

We can efficiently implement getMax of such data structure in -
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 38)

IDEA: StackWithMax will be implemented using a LinkedList where we add/remove nodes to/from front.

Third field of each node in the LinkedList will have max value in the stack from this node to the end.

When adding a new element, we compare the new element to max so far (in the third field), and set the maximum of them to be the max in the new node. getMax() function simply returns max in the third field of node in the linked list. Hence getMax() can efficiently be implemented in $\theta(1)$ time.

The queue is implemented using two stacks, denoted by $\text{incoming}$ and $\text{outgoing}$. The implementation rules are fixed as follows.

$$ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{Enqueue}(Q, x):\\ &\quad \text{Push } x \text{ into } \text{incoming} \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{Dequeue}(Q):\\ &\quad \textbf{if } \text{outgoing} \neq \varnothing \textbf{ then}\\ &\quad\quad \text{Pop and return the top element}\\ &\quad\quad \text{from } \text{outgoing}\\ &\quad \textbf{else}\\ &\quad\quad \text{Do Something (Which is not }\\ &\quad\quad \text{given to you) }\\ &\quad\quad \text{Return the required element}\\ &\quad \textbf{end if} \end{aligned} $$

Let $n$ enqueue operations and exactly $1$ dequeue operation are performed in some sequence.
Using the above implementation, determine the minimum and maximum number of pop operations possible.
(Maximum pop means there exists a sequence of enqueue and dequeue operations for which the number of pop operations cannot be less than the stated maximum.)

A queue is simulated using two stacks.

Here, say we name one stack as incoming and other as outgoing.

To enqueue in queue, we simply push elements in incoming.

To dequeue we first check if outgoing is empty. If it is not empty then we simply pop from outgoing. But if it is empty then we pop one by one all elements from incoming to outgoing and after that we pop one element from outgoing and return it.

n enqueue and 1 dequeue operations has been performed in some order.

To get minium number of pop operations, the sequence of enqueue and dequeue operations is – 

1 enqueue, 1 dequeue, n-1 enqueue.

This sequence is fixed for getting minimum pop.

minimum pop = 2.

To get maximum number of pop operations, the sequence of enqueue and dequeue operations is – 

n enqueue, 1 dequeue.

This sequence is fixed for getting maximum pop.

maximum pop = n+1.

Note : The above answers are true for above mentioned implementation. But the options don't match, so we've to think of something else.

The sequence of enqueue and dequeue is fixed for getting both minimum and maximum number of pop operations.

We've modified our dequeue operation, to see if we can reach to some conclusions - 

​​​To dequeue we first check if outgoing is empty. If it is not empty then we simply pop from outgoing.

But if it is empty, and say there are p elements in incoming then we pop one by one (p-1) elements from incoming to outgoing and pop pth element from incoming and return it.

This way we decreased the pop operations by 1.

Therefore, minimum pop = 1, maximum pop = n.

Answer :- A.

Note : Option B cannot be the answer, why?

To get minimum pop = 1, the sequence of enqueue and dequeue is fixed and is 1 enqueue, 1 dequeue, n-1 enqueue.

Internally you're doing 1 push in incoming stack, 1 pop from incoming stack (when size of incoming is 1), n-1 push in incoming stack.

To get maximum pop = n-1, the sequence of enqueue and dequeue is fixed and is n enqueue, 1 dequeue.

Internally you're doing n push in incoming stack, then n times pop from incoming and push to outgoing, then 1 pop from outgoing.

​​​​​​But this is contradictory. One time, to suit your requirement, you're saying for dequeue operation if size of incoming stack is 1 then pop from incoming stack. Other time, to suit your requirement, you're saying for dequeue operation first empty contents of incoming stack to outgoing stack then pop from outgoing stack.

To be precise, you're have 2 different contradictory behaviour when incoming stack size is 1.

Minimum pop: The minimum pop operation needed is 1. This happens whenever we perform the dequeue operation, and Stack 2 is not empty. In this case, we directly pop the front element from Stack 2 without transferring any elements from Stack 1.

Maximum pop: The maximum pop operation needed is n. This occurs when we perform the dequeue operation, and Stack 2 is empty. In this case, we need to transfer all n elements from Stack 1 to Stack 2, but after that, we only pop the front element from Stack 2. This process will require n pop operations.

So, the correct answer is:
Minimum pop = 1
Maximum pop = n.

Based on the analysis of the queue implementation using two stacks, here is the step-by-step solution:

1. Understanding the Implementation

The queue is implemented using two stacks:

  • incoming: Used for Enqueue operations (pushing new elements).

  • outgoing: Used for Dequeue operations (popping elements).

Operations:

  • Enqueue(x): Pushes x onto the incoming stack. (Cost: 0 pops, 1 push).

  • Dequeue():

    • Case 1: If outgoing is not empty, pop from outgoing.

    • Case 2: If outgoing is empty, execute "Do Something" (transfer elements from incoming to outgoing), then return the element.

The "Do Something" (Transfer) Logic:

To maintain FIFO (First-In-First-Out) order using LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) stacks, the standard transfer logic is:

  • Pop all elements from incoming.

  • Push them onto outgoing.

  • This reverses the order, so the bottom of incoming becomes the top of outgoing.

2. Analyzing the Scenarios

We perform $n$ enqueue operations and 1 dequeue operation in "some sequence".

Since outgoing is initially empty and we only dequeue once, the Dequeue operation must trigger the transfer ("Do Something") block.

Let $k$ be the number of elements in the incoming stack at the moment the Dequeue is called.

  • The Dequeue operation will transfer these $k$ elements.

  • Number of Pops for Transfer: We pop $k$ times from incoming.

  • Number of Pops to Return: After transfer, we pop 1 time from outgoing to return the value.

  • Total Pops for Dequeue: $k + 1$.

Note: In many academic contexts (like GATE), "number of pop operations" in this specific 2-stack problem often refers to the elements moved (transfer cost) or pops from the input stack, as the final pop is constant O(1). Let's check the bounds.

Scenario A: Minimum Pops

To minimize the pops, we need to minimize $k$ (the number of elements in incoming when we dequeue).

  • Sequence: Enqueue(1) $\rightarrow$ Dequeue() $\rightarrow$ Enqueue(n-1).

  • At the time of Dequeue, incoming has 1 element ($k=1$).

  • Action:

    1. Pop 1 element from incoming (Transfer).

    2. Push 1 element to outgoing.

    3. Pop 1 element from outgoing (Return).

  • Standard Count: $1 + 1 = 2$ pops.

  • "Transfer Cost" Count: 1 pop.

Scenario B: Maximum Pops

To maximize the pops, we need to maximize $k$.

  • Sequence: Enqueue(n) (all $n$ items) $\rightarrow$ Dequeue().

  • At the time of Dequeue, incoming has $n$ elements ($k=n$).

  • Action:

    1. Pop $n$ elements from incoming (Transfer).

    2. Push $n$ elements to outgoing.

    3. Pop 1 element from outgoing (Return).

  • Standard Count: $n + 1$ pops.

  • "Transfer Cost" Count: $n$ pops.

3. Matching with Options

Let's look at the ranges derived from the two counting interpretations:

  1. Strict Counting (Transfer + Return): Range is $[2, n+1]$.

    • No option matches this exactly.

  2. Transfer/Incoming Counting (Only Transfer): Range is $[1, n]$.

    • Matches Option A exactly.

Given that Option B is $[1, n+1]$, it would require inconsistent logic (ignoring the return pop for the minimum case but counting it for the maximum case). Option A is consistent in counting the variable cost (the transfer pops) which ranges from 1 to $n$.

Therefore, the question focuses on the number of pops required to move the data from incoming to outgoing.

  • Minimum: 1 pop (when 1 element is transferred).

  • Maximum: $n$ pops (when $n$ elements are transferred).

Conclusion

The correct option is A.

A. Minimum pop = 1, Maximum pop = n

  • If you count total pops, the answer should be Min=2, Max=n+1.

  • If you count transfer pops only, the answer is Min=1, Max=n.

Which of the following is/are correct ?
questions.solution:

Selected solution (score: 43)

STEP 1 :- Push the first integer of array directly to the stack.

STEP 2 :- Now start traversing the array elements from second element till the last element one by one and follow the following steps in loop :- 

  • mark the current element as NEXT. 
  • If stack is not empty, compare the top element of stack with NEXT.
  • If NEXT is greater than the top element of stack, Pop element from stack. NEXT is the next nearest greater element for the popped element.
  • Keep popping from the stack while the popped element is smaller than NEXT , NEXT becomes the next nearest greater element for all such popped elements.
  • If NEXT is smaller than the top element of stack then simply push the NEXT in the stack or if the stack become empty after popping of elements then simply push NEXT in stack. 

STEP 3 :- After the loop in step 2 is over, pop all the elements from the stack and print -1 for all those element at their’s respective position as no nearest greater element exist for them on right side of them.

 

Ex :- 

Let our array be: $\rightarrow$

$$A[6] \Rightarrow \begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline 5 & 6 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 7 \\\hline\end{array}$$

Step 1:- Push 5 i.e. $A[0]$ to stack

$$\text { Stack } \Rightarrow 5$$

Step 2 : Compare $A[1]$ with top of stack

$$6>5$$

$\therefore$ pop from stack and push 6 in stack and nearest greater element for $A[0]$ will be $6$

Step 3:- Compare $A[2]$ with top of stack

$$3<6$$

$\therefore$ push $A[2]$ to the stack

$$\text { Stack } \Rightarrow 63$$

Step 4:- Compare A[3] with top of stack

$$2<3$$

$\therefore$ push $A[3]$ to the stack

$$\text { Stack } \rightarrow 632$$

Step 5:- Compare A[4] with top of stack

$$1<2$$

$\therefore$ Push A $[4]$ to the stack.

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad 6321$$

Step 6:- Compare A[5] with top of stack.

$$7>1$$

$\Rightarrow$ pop the top of stack and update its place's value in array with 7 as it will be its nearest greater element.

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad 632$$

again compare A [5] with top of stack

 $$7>2$$

$\Rightarrow$ pop and replace 2 in array with 7.

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad 63$$

again compare A[5] with top of stack

$$7>3$$

$\Rightarrow$ pop and replace 3 in array with 7

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad 6$$

again compare A[5] with top of stack

$$7>6$$

$\Rightarrow$ pop and replace 6 in array with 7

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad $$

As stack got empty push $A[5]$ in stack

$$\text { Stack }\Rightarrow \quad 7$$

Now no new element present to traverse in array.Therefore pop from stack untill it gets empty and replace all the values present in the stack with $-1$ in the main array as there does not exist any nearest greater element for them.

$$\text{final array} \Rightarrow \quad\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline 6 & 7 & 7 & 7 & 7 & -1 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Analysis of Options:

Consider a stack S that stores integers.

The operation  push(S, i) returns a new stack obtained by inserting integer $i$ on top of S.

For example:

options.html: If <i>S</i> is empty, then after <i>S</i> = <code>push(S, 2)</code>, the $\text{push(S, 2)}$ operation returns the new stack [2], so <i>S</i> becomes [2].
After one more push: <i>S</i> = <code>push(S, 3)</code> the $\text{push(S, 3)}$ operation returns the new stack [2,3], so <i>S</i> becomes [2, 3].

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 30)

  1. $f(\operatorname{push}(S, 2))=2^{\max \{0,0\}}+2=3$
  2. $f(\operatorname{push}(S, 1))=2^{\max \{3,0\}}-1=7$
  3. $f(\operatorname{push}(S, 2))=2^{\max \{7,0\}}+2=130$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Problem Analysis:

We need to calculate the value of $f(S)$ for a stack $S$ built by pushing elements [2, 1, 2] (from bottom to top).

  • $f(\text{empty}) = 0$

  • Recursive step depends on whether the pushed element $i$ is even or odd.

Calculation:

  1. Start: $S = \text{empty}$. $f(S) = 0$.

  2. Push 2 (Bottom element): $i = 2$ (Even).

     

    $$f(S) = 2^{\max(0, 0)} + 2 = 2^0 + 2 = 1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}$$

  3. Push 1: $i = 1$ (Odd).

     

    $$f(S) = 2^{\max(3, 0)} - 1 = 2^3 - 1 = 8 - 1 = \mathbf{7}$$

  4. Push 2 (Top element): $i = 2$ (Even).

     

    $$f(S) = 2^{\max(7, 0)} + 2 = 2^7 + 2 = 128 + 2 = \mathbf{130}$$

Answer: D. 130

we need to print the queue elements in reverse order ($5, 4, 3, 2, 1$) using only the standard queue operations: enqueue(), dequeue(), and print().

To solve this without extra storage, we must rotate the queue. A single rotation consists of one dequeue() immediately followed by an enqueue(), which moves the front element to the back.

The Logic

To print any element that is not at the head, we must rotate the elements in front of it to the back. In a queue of size $N=5$:

Bringing the $k$-th element to the head: Requires moving $k-1$ elements to the back.

Cost of one rotation: $1 \text{ dequeue} + 1 \text{ enqueue} = 2 \text{ calls}$.

Cost of printing: $1 \text{ print call}$.

Step-by-Step Execution

Initial State: $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$ (1 is at the head)

To Print '5': * Rotate elements $1, 2, 3, 4$ to the back ($4$ rotations).

Calls: $4 \times 2 = 8$ calls.

Queue state: $[5, 1, 2, 3, 4]$.

Call print(): $1$ call.

Subtotal: 9 calls. (Current Output: 5)

To Print '4': * In the current state $[5, 1, 2, 3, 4]$, '4' is at the tail.

Rotate $5, 1, 2, 3$ to the back ($4$ rotations).

Calls: $4 \times 2 = 8$ calls.

Queue state: $[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]$.

Call print(): $1$ call.

Subtotal: 9 calls. (Current Output: 5, 4)

To Print '3': * '3' is now at the tail of $[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]$.

Rotate 4 times ($4, 5, 1, 2$ to back) + print().

Subtotal: 9 calls. (Current Output: 5, 4, 3)

To Print '2': * '2' is now at the tail of $[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]$.

Rotate 4 times ($3, 4, 5, 1$ to back) + print().

Subtotal: 9 calls. (Current Output: 5, 4, 3, 2)

To Print '1': * '1' is now at the tail of $[2, 3, 4, 5, 1]$.

Rotate 4 times ($2, 3, 4, 5$ to back) + print().

Subtotal: 9 calls. (Current Output: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1)

Final Result

Final Queue State: $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$ (This matches the initial content requirement).

Total Calls: $9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = \mathbf{45}$

The total number of calls required is 45.
